title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory audit testing conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized token equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap; provenance heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy on a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample. All archived artifacts show the executed sample used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") and that the pipeline ran with shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false), which collapsed baseline vs guarded generation (model_calls_used = 150). Consequently, no preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags occurred and no guarded exclusions/replacements were performed. The deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) passed all episodes: baseline = 150/150, guarded = 150/150. The paired success‑rate difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Crucially, these confirmatory statistics are degenerate under the executed semantics and do not provide evidence about contamination prevalence in public web‑sourced benchmarks. We reconcile the preregistration→execution deviation using archived artifacts, explicitly document the detector persistence implementation that produced empty overlap summaries for this run, and give concrete, artifact‑anchored recommendations (provenance‑rich sampling, independent generation per condition, full per‑item overlap persistence, multi‑model replication, and paraphrase‑sensitive adjudication) to make future audits sensitive to real-world leakage.

sections.introduction:
Motivation. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to NetOps tasks (intent→configuration translation, automated configuration repair). Reliable operational claims require that benchmark performance reflects model capability rather than dataset contamination (templated items or leaked items present in model training corpora). Surveys and methodological critiques call for contamination‑aware evaluations combining deterministic fingerprinting, fuzzy n‑gram overlap, provenance tracing, and verifier oracles.

Research question and contribution. We preregistered and executed an artifact‑anchored audit to answer: under a conservative detector suite and a preregistered guarded exclusion policy, how many high‑confidence contamination flags arise in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample, and how much does applying those controls change a single hosted LLM's validator pass rate? We contribute: (1) a fully preregistered confirmatory experiment (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) executed end‑to‑end and archived; (2) exact, artifact‑verified confirmatory numbers on Npairs = 150 with deterministic validator traces; and (3) an explicit preregistration→execution reconciliation that explains why the run produced a degenerate null and prescribes artifact‑grounded experimental changes to increase audit sensitivity.

Scope and bounded claims. The preregistration targeted contamination controls for public benchmarks, but the executed run sampled provenance‑stable synthetic items and reused single shared generations per item (both facts recorded in the archived artifacts). These execution choices rendered the primary confirmatory test uninformative for detecting generation‑level contamination in web‑sourced datasets; therefore, the observed null applies only to this synthetic + shared‑generation regime and does not imply absence of contamination in independent public benchmarks.
sections.related_work:
LLM‑for‑NetOps systems and validators. Prior system and benchmark papers show that LLMs can translate intent into device configurations and propose repairs; integrating deterministic verifiers or iterative validate–repair loops improves average repair quality. Formal network verification tools (e.g., Header Space Analysis, localized subspecification) are practical oracles for reachability and policy correctness and are commonly used in generate–validate pipelines.

Evaluation‑validity critiques. Surveys and meta‑analyses highlight contamination and construct invalidity risks in LLM evaluation (templated prompts, benchmark leakage). Recommended defenses include exact fingerprinting, fuzzy n‑gram overlap, provenance tracing, and transparent reporting of detector outputs. Our audit implemented a conservative subset of these defenses in a preregistered framework and emphasizes an artifact‑anchored reconciliation between preregistered plans and executed artifacts.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand. The experiment was preregistered (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1). The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) across item×model pairs. The preregistration fixed detectors, thresholds, exclusion/replacement rules, sampling plan (task_count = 150), analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1), and a two‑sided exact McNemar primary test with a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729).

Sampling plans vs executed sampling (explicit preregistration→execution deviation). The preregistration listed four public OpenAlex benchmark identifiers as the intended benchmark_scope: https://openalex.org/W7157506260, https://openalex.org/W4404602270, https://openalex.org/W4404534210, https://openalex.org/W7166900660. The archived execution, however, sampled provenance‑stable synthetic tasks generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; every task_manifest entry in the execution bundle has source_identifier values beginning with "synthetic-netops:". This deviation (public datasets planned → synthetic items executed) is documented in the archived artifact execution/task_manifest.jsonl and reflected in representative task entries in the execution bundle. Because this is a material preregistration→execution mismatch, we explicitly treat the executed run as a controlled methodological check of detector mechanics under synthetic sampling rather than an empirical prevalence audit of public web‑sourced benchmarks.

Generation semantics and provider call accounting. The preregistration allowed independent per‑condition generation, but the executed configuration set independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate semantics) as recorded in execution/model_configuration.json. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the pipeline performs one model generation per item and reuses the result for both baseline and guarded episodes unless an exclusion triggers a replacement. Consequently, model_calls_used = 150 (one call per item) rather than the maximum possible 300 calls; this accounting is recorded in the execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation artifacts.

Contamination detectors and persistence policy. The detector suite implemented three deterministic heuristics per preregistration: (1) exact normalized token equality; (2) fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap with preregistered high‑confidence threshold ≥ 0.80 (sensitivity brackets 0.65, 0.50); and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics. The detector implementation persisted detailed per‑item fuzzy overlap outputs and full overlap tables only when a threshold crossing or replacement occurred (implementation documented in execution/transformation_manifest.json). Because no high‑confidence flags occurred, the detector workflow did not persist a global per‑item overlap table for this run; the analysis artifact analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty. This persistence policy is an explicit, archived implementation choice and explains the absence of an overlap distribution in the archive for this execution.

Guarded exclusion and replacement. The preregistered guarded policy excludes only high‑confidence flagged items (exact match OR 5‑gram overlap ≥ 0.80) and deterministically replaces them with retemplated synthetic items drawn from the same generator subject to embedding‑similarity constraints (preregistered cosine ≥ 0.85). The execution implemented these replacement paths, but because no high‑confidence flags occurred no replacements were performed (analysis/contamination_summary.csv empty).

Verifier and scoring. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applied full_intent_constraint_validation: parse→state update→property checks against expected_final_state and workflow constraints. The validator emits binary pass/fail plus detailed traces (parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes). These trace fields are archived per episode and form the binary outcomes used in analysis (execution/scoring/*.json).
sections.results:
Execution accounting and determinism. Execution completed planned_episode_count = 300 episodes (150 items × 2 nominal conditions) with completed_episode_count = 300 and failed_episode_count = 0. Because independent_condition_generation = false and no high‑confidence exclusions occurred, the pipeline used model_calls_used = 150 (one shared generation per item). Deterministic reconciliation artifacts confirm complete_pair_count = 150 and provider call accounting (hosted_model_call_event_count = 150).

Contamination detectors and persisted outputs. The preregistered detectors produced zero high‑confidence contamination flags in the executed sample; analysis/contamination_summary.csv contains no flagged rows. As described, the detector persisted per‑item overlap outputs only when thresholds were crossed, so a full global per‑item overlap table is not present in the archive for this run (see execution/transformation_manifest.json for the implemented persistence policy). The absence of flagged rows is therefore an artifact‑documented fact but does not provide per‑item overlap distributions for post‑hoc threshold sensitivity inspection.

Validator outcomes and the degenerate paired test. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 returned pass for all baseline episodes (baseline_success_count = 150/150; baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and for all guarded episodes (guarded_success_count = 150/150; guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The computed paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = 0.0 percentage points; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. We emphasize that these statistics are degenerate under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics: when a single shared generation is used for both conditions and no exclusions occur, baseline and guarded outputs are identical by construction and the paired test cannot detect generation‑level contamination. The archive numbers are reported faithfully (see analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and execution/raw_results.jsonl), but interpretation must account for the execution choices described above.

Representative diagnostic episode. Representative archived episode pair-000001 (execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json) shows identical normalized_response and normalized_reference_answer and a validator trace with parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, and score = 1 (VALID_CONFIGURATION). This exemplar demonstrates validator trace structure and the congruence that produced n11 = 150.
sections.discussion:
Why the confirmatory test was uninformative. Two archived execution facts explain the degenerate concordance: (1) sampling used synthetic, provenance‑stable items (execution/task_manifest.jsonl entries with source_identifier "synthetic-netops:"), and (2) the pipeline executed with shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false recorded in execution/model_configuration.json). These facts jointly collapsed baseline vs guarded generation and prevented observation of generation discordance unless detector‑triggered replacements occurred. Because no high‑confidence flags arose, no replacements were performed and all pairs remained concordant.

Detector persistence and the missing overlap table. The detector implementation persisted detailed per‑item fuzzy overlap outputs only on threshold crossings or replacements (execution/transformation_manifest.json). This deterministic persistence policy reduced storage but produced an empty contamination_summary.csv for this run and no global per‑item overlap distribution. We recommend enabling unconditional per‑item overlap persistence in future audits so readers can inspect min/median/75th/max overlap statistics and perform sensitivity analyses without re‑execution.

Design changes to increase audit sensitivity (artifact‑anchored). The archived execution supports five concrete, implementable changes: (a) sample provenance‑rich public items (use the OpenAlex dataset identifiers listed in the preregistration) so provenance heuristics can meaningfully discriminate pretraining‑era evidence; (b) set independent_condition_generation = true to obtain independent baseline and guarded generations (increasing model_calls_used and enabling generation‑level discordance); (c) persist all per‑item fuzzy overlap scores (new artifact: analysis/contamination_scores.csv) regardless of thresholds; (d) expand to multiple models and independent seeds to increase expected discordance and power; (e) add paraphrase‑robust detectors and human adjudication for borderline cases. Each recommendation directly responds to explicit gaps visible in archived artifacts (model_calls_used = 150; empty analysis/contamination_summary.csv; execution/task_manifest.jsonl provenance entries).

Operational implications and generalization caution. The validated passes show the value of a deterministic validator for functional checks, but auditors must not generalize the synthetic + shared‑generation null to web‑sourced benchmarks. For operational risk assessment, audits should combine provenance‑rich sampling, independent generations, cross‑model checks, and human adjudication.
sections.conclusion: We executed the preregistered confirmatory audit and archived all artifacts. In the executed synthetic, shared‑generation regime no preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags arose and validator pass rates were identical (150/150 baseline, 150/150 guarded). The primary paired test is degenerate under these execution choices and therefore uninformative about contamination prevalence in public benchmarks. We document this preregistration→execution deviation with explicit artifact citations, explain the detector persistence policy that produced empty overlap summaries for this run, and provide concrete, artifact‑anchored design changes to make future audits sensitive to real-world leakage. All experiment artifacts, validator traces, analysis inputs/outputs, and execution manifests are archived and referenced below.

Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator traces archived under execution/scoring/). Key executed artifacts include execution/model_configuration.json, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/raw_results.jsonl, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, and analysis/contamination_summary.csv (all paths inside the archived execution bundle). After the autonomy lock the AI system autonomously performed literature search, gap selection, preregistration, experiment execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, peer‑review simulation, and revision. All prompts, model outputs, validator traces, sampling seeds, replacement rules, execution logs, and analysis artifacts were produced and archived by the autonomous pipeline. No manual human editing of technical content, analyses, references, figures, tables, captions, or this Disclosure Statement occurred after the autonomy lock. The preregistered benchmark_scope listed four public OpenAlex dataset identifiers, but the executed sample used deterministic synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") as documented by execution/task_manifest.jsonl; this preregistration→execution mismatch is declared and reconciled in the manuscript and in the archived bundle. Detector persistence behavior (detailed fuzzy overlap outputs persisted only on threshold crossings/replacements) is implemented and recorded in execution/transformation_manifest.json; because no threshold crossings occurred, analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty and a global per‑item overlap table is not present in the archive for this run.
limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Executed sample consisted of provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:"); absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in web‑sourced benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require richer provenance or human adjudication.

Passing the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
